newsitem.title: FRANCE: EU said asking French commitments on Thomson - paper.
newsitem.headline: EU said asking French commitments on Thomson - paper.

text.p: The European Commission has asked the French government to make a number of commitments on the competition aspects of the privatisation and recapitalisation of the Thomson SA electronics group, a French newspaper reported on Saturday.

Le Monde published what it said was a working paper dated November 26 from EU Commissioner on Competition Karel van Miert telling Finance Minister Jean Arthuis the commitments were needed by December 2 in order to avoid a lenghtier procedure.

It said van Miert sought a commitment that the market share of Thomson's Multimedia unit would be frozen at its current level until the indebted company returns to financial health, and that the restructuring plan would keep production capacity at its current level.

A report in the French daily La Tribune earlier this week said the Commission would give its view on the proposed acquisition of Thomson-CSF by Lagardere Groupe and the Multimedia unit of Daewoo Electronics on December 4.
It said the Commission will rule on the state's 11 billion franc capital injection into Thomson on December 18.
Le Monde said Arthuis had declined to confirm its report, but told it he was providing the Commission the information it needed to be able to give its views as soon as possible.
The expected dates for the Commission's statements could be delayed by three weeks if there are appeals on the competition issues and 10 days on the recapitalisation front, La Tribune said.
The Commission itself could also ask for more information which would give it a further three months to decide.
Lagardere's proposed acquisition of Thomson and Daewoo's control of Thomson Multimedia were notified to the Commission for clearance under the merger regulation on October 31.

A French association representing about 1,000 Thomson Multimedia employees has been lobbying the Commission, protesting against the privatisation procedure, on the grounds that it precluded a management buyout, posed competition problems and that there was a lack of investment reciprocity with South Korea.
